items.subtype_name: Common ground: what both authors accept
items.stimulus:
Text 1
When the province of Velmora raised its minimum wage by 12 percent in 2019, economist Daria Kossman tracked restaurant payrolls for two years. The number of restaurant employees stayed essentially flat. Kossman concluded that moderate wage increases need not cost low-wage workers their jobs.

Text 2
Kossman's count of Velmora's restaurant employees is careful, and few dispute that headcounts held steady. But headcount is not the whole story. Many Velmora restaurants trimmed weekly shifts after the increase, so workers kept their jobs while losing hours and, in some cases, income.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Moderate minimum wage increases do not harm low-wage workers.
Velmora's restaurant headcount held roughly steady after the increase.
Velmora restaurants cut workers' weekly shifts after the increase.
Two years is too short a period to judge a wage increase.
items.explanation: The texts disagree about whether the wage increase hurt workers. Underneath that disagreement, both accept the same fact. Text 1 reports that the number of restaurant employees 'stayed essentially flat,' and Text 2 grants that 'headcounts held steady.' You can point to a sentence in each text that supports this choice.

A.why: You picked Text 1's side of the disagreement. Text 2 argues that workers were harmed through lost hours and income, so its author would reject this statement.

C.why: Only Text 2 says restaurants cut shifts. Text 1 never mentions hours, so you can't credit this claim to both authors.

D.why: Neither text questions whether two years is long enough. You brought in a criticism that neither author makes.

items.subtype_name: Common ground: what both authors accept
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Versions of "The Lantern Bride," a tale about a woman who guides lost boats home, have been recorded in more than forty fishing villages along the Merrin coast. Folklorist Tomas Ehrlund notes that the versions share an unusually specific plot, and he argues that sailors carried a single original story from port to port.

Text 2
No one questions that the Merrin versions of "The Lantern Bride" are strikingly alike. Yet villages facing the same storms and the same losses at sea could simply have arrived at similar stories independently. Shared hardship, not shared sailors, may explain the resemblance.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Sailors spread one original version of the tale along the coast.
Communities facing similar dangers tend to invent similar stories.
The tale was first told in the largest Merrin fishing village.
Versions of the tale from different villages closely resemble one another.
items.explanation: The authors disagree about why the versions are similar. Both accept that they are similar. Text 1 says the versions 'share an unusually specific plot,' and Text 2 says 'no one questions' that they are 'strikingly alike.' That shared observation is the common ground.

A.why: This is Text 1's explanation, which is one side of the disagreement. Text 2 offers shared hardship as the cause instead, so its author would not sign on.

B.why: Only Text 2 proposes this, and only tentatively ('could simply'). Text 1 credits sailors, so this statement doesn't pass the check against both texts.

C.why: Neither text says where the tale began. Text 1 mentions 'a single original story' but never places it in a particular village.

items.subtype_name: Common ground: what both authors accept
items.stimulus:
Text 1
On shallow reefs off the Tarrow Islands, divers counted fish species on patches with and without cleaner wrasses, small fish that pick parasites off larger ones. Patches with wrasses consistently held more species. The research team concluded that cleaner wrasses raise fish diversity on coral reefs in general.

Text 2
The Tarrow finding for shallow reefs is solid: there, patches with cleaner wrasses do hold more species. On reefs deeper than 30 meters, however, surveys have found no such difference, so the team's conclusion may hold only for shallow water.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: On shallow Tarrow reefs, patches with cleaner wrasses held more fish species.
Cleaner wrasses raise fish diversity on coral reefs at every depth.
Deep reefs support fewer fish species overall than shallow reefs do.
Cleaner wrasses remove parasites mostly from the largest reef fish.
items.explanation: Text 2 narrows Text 1's broad conclusion, but it opens by granting the shallow-reef result: 'The Tarrow finding for shallow reefs is solid.' Text 1 reports that same result directly. So both authors accept that wrasse patches on shallow Tarrow reefs held more species.

B.why: This is Text 1's broad conclusion, and Text 2 disputes it directly by citing deep reefs where no difference appeared. You picked one side of the disagreement.

C.why: Text 2 says deep reefs show no difference between patches with and without wrasses. It says nothing about the total number of species at depth, and Text 1 doesn't either.

D.why: You latched onto Text 1's passing description of what wrasses do. Neither text says which fish they clean most, and Text 2 never discusses feeding at all.

items.subtype_name: Common ground: what both authors accept
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In the town of Halbrook, older residents pronounce "pin" and "pen" differently, but most younger residents do not. Linguist Ines Robart's recordings show that by the 1970s the two vowels had merged in the speech of most Halbrook teenagers. Robart therefore concludes that the merger began in the 1970s.

Text 2
Robart's recordings leave little doubt that the merger was common among Halbrook teenagers in the 1970s. But audio recordings made in the 1930s capture a handful of speakers already merging the vowels. The change likely began decades earlier and spread widely only later.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The merger of the two vowels in Halbrook began in the 1970s.
A few Halbrook speakers merged the vowels as early as the 1930s.
The merger was widespread among Halbrook teenagers by the 1970s.
Older Halbrook residents are now starting to merge the vowels too.
items.explanation: The disagreement is about when the merger began. Both texts accept that it was common among teenagers by the 1970s. Text 1 says it had merged 'in the speech of most Halbrook teenagers,' and Text 2 says there is 'little doubt' the merger was common then.

A.why: This is Robart's conclusion, which Text 2 was written to dispute. You picked one side of the disagreement instead of the ground the two sides share.

B.why: Only Text 2 cites the 1930s recordings. Text 1 never mentions them, and its conclusion implies the merger did not exist that early.

D.why: Text 1 says older residents still pronounce the words differently, and Text 2 says nothing about older speakers changing. Nothing in either text supports this.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
Inspectors of the Ferris Street Bridge traced its widening cracks to corroded steel reinforcing bars inside the concrete deck, where decades of winter road salt had seeped in. The firm overseeing repairs therefore recommends replacing the damaged bars with epoxy-coated steel, which resists salt.

Text 2
The inspectors are right that road salt corroded the Ferris Street Bridge's reinforcing steel. Epoxy-coated bars, though, are a weak remedy: their coating is often nicked during installation, and corrosion concentrates at those nicks. Stainless steel bars would last far longer.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Epoxy-coated bars are the best replacement for the damaged steel.
Road salt contributed to corrosion of the bridge's reinforcing steel.
Epoxy coatings are often damaged while the bars are being installed.
The bridge's cracks were caused mainly by heavy truck traffic.
items.explanation: Text 2 begins with a concession: 'The inspectors are right that road salt corroded' the steel. Text 1 traces the damage to road salt. The authors disagree only about the fix, so the cause of the corrosion is their common ground.

A.why: This is the firm's recommendation in Text 1. Text 2 calls epoxy 'a weak remedy,' so you picked the point the two texts disagree about.

C.why: Only Text 2 raises the problem of nicked coatings. Text 1 presents epoxy as salt-resistant and never mentions installation damage.

D.why: Both texts blame road salt for the damage. Neither mentions truck traffic, so this choice conflicts with what each author says.

Text 1
In a trial of a new nasal-spray flu vaccine, volunteers aged 18 to 50 developed strong antibody responses within two weeks. Because the spray is painless and easy to give, the trial's authors conclude that it should replace flu injections for adults.

The nasal spray's results in younger adults are impressive. Adults over 65, however, were not in the trial, and their immune systems often respond weakly to nasal vaccines. For them, the injection may remain the better choice.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The nasal spray should replace flu injections for adults of all ages.
Older adults often respond weakly to vaccines given as a nasal spray.
The nasal spray protects against more flu strains than injections do.
Trial volunteers aged 18 to 50 responded strongly to the nasal spray.

B.why: Only Text 2 makes this claim about older adults. Text 1 says nothing about how people over 65 respond.

C.why: Neither text mentions flu strains. Text 1 prefers the spray because it is painless and easy to give, not because it covers more strains.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
Records kept since 1994 show that Ashby warblers now reach their breeding grounds in Quebec about nine days earlier than they once did. Over the same period, spring temperatures there have risen. Ornithologist Lena Varga concludes that warmer springs on the breeding grounds are drawing the birds north sooner.

Text 2
There is no question that Ashby warblers are arriving earlier. But a warbler wintering in Central America cannot sense the temperature in Quebec. Warmer conditions along its migration route, which let it refuel faster, could have produced the same earlier arrival.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Warmer springs in Quebec are causing the warblers to arrive earlier.
Faster refueling along the route has shortened the warblers' migration.
Ashby warblers now reach their breeding grounds earlier than in 1994.
Earlier arrival has reduced the warblers' breeding success in Quebec.

A.why: This is Varga's conclusion, and Text 2 argues against it, saying the birds can't sense Quebec temperatures. You picked one side of the disagreement.

B.why: Only Text 2 suggests this, and it says only that it 'could have' happened. Text 1 never mentions conditions along the route.

items.subtype_name: Common ground: what both authors accept
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Seismologist Tomás Ferreira studied the months before four major earthquakes along a Pacific fault. Before each one, sensors recorded a swarm of small tremors near the future epicenter. Ferreira therefore suggests that closely watching such swarms could help scientists forecast large earthquakes.

Text 2
It is true that swarms of small tremors came before the earthquakes Ferreira examined. But swarms are common, and the great majority of them fade away with no large earthquake following. A warning sign that is usually followed by nothing gives forecasters little to go on.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Watching tremor swarms is a reliable way for scientists to forecast large earthquakes.
Most tremor swarms along faults end without any large earthquake following them.
Swarms of small tremors came before the major earthquakes in Ferreira's study.
Sensors along Pacific faults should be replaced with more sensitive equipment.
items.explanation: The authors disagree about whether swarms are useful for forecasting. Underneath that, both accept what Ferreira observed: Text 1 says sensors recorded a swarm 'before each one,' and Text 2 begins 'It is true that swarms of small tremors came before the earthquakes Ferreira examined.' That concession is the shared ground.

A.why: Text 2 rejects this outright, saying such a sign 'gives forecasters little to go on.' It also overstates Text 1, which only says watching swarms 'could help.' You picked a stronger version of one side of the disagreement.

choices: Streetlights shift robins' daily rhythms, which causes earlier dawn song.
Robins in lit areas start their dawn song earlier than robins in dark ones.
Morning traffic noise can make robin song harder for other birds to hear.
Robins in quiet, dark fields sing more loudly than robins in towns do.
items.explanation: The authors disagree about why urban robins sing earlier: light in Text 1, traffic noise in Text 2. Both accept the observation itself. Text 1 reports that robins near streetlights began singing 'up to forty minutes before' robins in dark fields, and Text 2 says this 'is not in question.' The same observation is given two explanations, so the observation is the common ground.

A.why: This is Text 1's explanation, and Text 2 offers a rival one that the lighting data 'cannot rule out.' You picked one side of the disagreement.

C.why: Only Text 2 raises traffic noise. Text 1 never mentions it, so you can't point to a sentence showing that author would agree. Check every choice against both texts.

D.why: Neither text compares how loudly robins sing in different places. Text 2 is about when robins sing, not how loudly. You drew an inference neither passage supports.
